Basic Safety Message (BSM) classification for anomaly detection is modeled as a distributed learning problem over a vehicular network with dynamic topology. As a critical threat to FL, a feature-space clean-label attack is introduced, wherein benign samples are perturbed toward malicious feature extremes, degrading class separability while preserving labels. To counter this, a feature-consistency relabeling defense is proposed to detect and relabel suspicious samples. A game-theoretic framework is developed to capture attack-defense interactions and characterize equilibrium strategies based on attack effectiveness and cost parameters. Results show that the attack scales effectively with compromised nodes, while the proposed defense keeps attack success low without degrading clean accuracy and shifts equilibrium regions toward attack-averse regimes. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models
docs.text:
On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models On-Policy Self-Training: Data-Free Self-Improvement in Large Language Models arXiv:2610.32770v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: On-policy self-distillation enables post-training foundation models without relying on stronger external teachers. However, existing approaches rely on ground-truth question-answer pairs, human-curated problem sets, or other supervised signals. In this work, we reformulate on-policy self-distillation as a self-training framework, driven by self-generated question-answer pairs and privileged reasoning demonstrations. We push supervision to the limit: guided solely by coarse, high-level topic descriptions, the model synthesizes its own curriculum of queries and privileged reasoning traces without access to any human-curated prompts or answers. We find that self-distillation on fully synthetic privileged information enables a model to improve across multiple domains while retaining its capabilities on domains it is not self-trained on. We demonstrate the generality of this framework across text and multimodal domains, achieving consistent self-improvement on standard language benchmarks and Visual Question Answering. Our findings demonstrate that foundation models possess rich latent capabilities that can be amplified without external task supervision or curated problem distributions. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
docs.text:
Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary arXiv:2610.32788v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $\alpha=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $\alpha/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $\alpha_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation
docs.text:
Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation Singular Geometry of Low-Rank Adaptation arXiv:2610.32854v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is now a standard approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large neural networks. Its low-rank factorization is inherently non-identifiable, making LoRA a singular statistical model whose learning complexity cannot be described by parameter dimension alone. We study this complexity using the real log canonical threshold (RLCT) from singular learning theory and how it depends on both the low-rank parameterization and the pretrained network. Under a local linearization, LoRA induces a low-rank trace regression model whose Kullback--Leibler geometry is controlled by a forward-backward covariance, constructed from activations and backpropagated sensitivities at the adapted layer. This covariance determines which low-rank perturbations are statistically observable. When it is nondegenerate along the relevant low-rank directions, we recover the classical learning complexity of reduced-rank regression; when its kernel meets these directions, additional statistically indistinguishable parameters change the singular geometry. We characterize this geometry locally through observable tangent directions and a residual singularity, and globally through affine linear sections of determinantal varieties. The global learning complexity need not be determined at a ground-truth parameter, as singularities on another rank stratum can dominate. We also introduce a curvature-corrected multi-temperature estimator of the RLCT. Experiments on multilayer perceptron and transformer architectures reveal strongly layer-dependent forward-backward geometry and show that ambient covariance degeneracy does not imply degeneracy along the low-rank directions relevant to adaptation. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence
docs.text:
Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence Trusting the Tool: Asymmetric Deference of LLM Vulnerability Auditors to Static-Analysis Evidence arXiv:2610.32876v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Pipelines that combine large language models (LLMs) with static analysis let the model consume the analyser's output as evidence, but whether the model distinguishes true from false evidence, and whether its scrutiny depends on what the evidence claims, has not been measured. We built an intraprocedural analyser for C/C++ that produces proof obligations and audited vulnerable and patched functions from PrimeVul under six evidence conditions that differ only in the notes, including fabricated assurances that a missing check exists and fabricated alarms that an added check is missing. The study covers 916 pairs in four disjoint sets, eleven model configurations from four vendors and 16,572 audits; no model is trained or fine-tuned. True evidence barely improved accuracy (+0.02). False evidence acted asymmetrically: relative to true notes about the same operations, false assurances lowered the detection of real vulnerabilities by up to 19 points, whereas false alarms never significantly lowered accuracy and were disputed far more often. An internally registered replication on seven new models confirmed that false assurances move verdicts towards their claim more than false alarms do (mean asymmetry +0.16, 95% CI +0.10 to +0.24). Instructions in the audit prompt did not reliably reduce deference; the best one failed to replicate. Verifying each claim in a separate call and showing the refuted claims raised accuracy under false assurances by 12 points in a pre-specified test (p=0.002) without loss under true evidence; for a second model the gain was smaller and not significant. Pipelines should therefore verify a tool's guarantees before the model relies on them, and studies should measure deference in a direction-aware way. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation
docs.text:
When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation When Human Corrections Travel: Safety in Federated VLA Adaptation arXiv:2610.32888v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders
docs.text:
LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders LoCA: Enabling Multi-Modality in Geospatial Location Encoders arXiv:2610.32894v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Location encoders map geographic coordinates to high-dimensional descriptors through contrastive alignment with paired Earth Observation imagery. We prove that this construction is structurally limited: any Lipschitz location encoder produces an output of intrinsic dimension at most 2, regardless of architecture or bandwidth, which forces the contrastive loss to strictly exceed its asymptotic optimum. Empirically, joint training also collapses the encoder's embedding covariance to low rank. Although dimension-limited, current location encoders sidestep this spectral collapse by training against a frozen image encoder, which we reinterpret as a covariance regularizer that supplies a high-rank target for the location encoder to fold onto. However, extending this approach to multimodal inputs is challenging, as location encoders should simultaneously map a single location to multiple, potentially incompatible, descriptors. We identify two requirements a regularizer must satisfy for location encoding in multimodal regimes: co-alignment across modalities, since adapters alone cannot align independently pretrained encoders; and high effective rank, since the location encoder inherits its target's spectrum. We propose LoCA (Location Contrastive Alignment), a two-stage pipeline that satisfies both. Stage 1 jointly trains Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 encoders with contrastive learning, producing a co-aligned, high-rank multimodal target. Stage 2 freezes the image encoders and trains a location and a tabular metadata encoder as projection adapters with multi-view contrastive learning. Against five state-of-the-art encoders on 17 tasks ranging from land cover and wildfire forecasting to geophysical, socio-economic, biodiversity and climate applications, LoCA achieves the most task wins, is the only model to outperform every other on a majority of tasks, and wins 68.8% of all per-task comparisons. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
docs.text:
SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements arXiv:2610.32919v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora
docs.text:
Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding for Mixed Natural Language and Structured Symbolic Corpora arXiv:2610.32921v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Modern language models rely on subwording tokenization to define the discrete units of input processing, typically using methods like Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) that treat whitespace as a fixed semantic boundary. This design is inherently limited, as many meaningful concepts---including multiword expressions and the structured environments of formal languages like LaTeX---frequently span across whitespaces. While recent superword tokenization methods attempt to address this by relaxing whitespace constraints, they often rely on greedy frequency-driven merging that fails to account for token length or the specific needs of underrepresented domain-specific languages. In this paper, we introduce Adaptive Frequency Threshold Byte Pair Encoding (AdaBPE), a new tokenization method that leverages an adaptive frequent-pattern mining approach. AdaBPE features a twofold dynamicity: it adapts minimum frequency thresholds based on both the length of a candidate token, to prevent favoring frequent short patterns, and its type, to distinguish between general and formal language patterns, using LaTeX as case in point. This allows the model to efficiently allocate vocabulary capacity to domain-specific notations, such as LaTeX, even when they represent a small fraction of the training data. We evaluate AdaBPE across five datasets spanning LaTeX and natural language, showing consistent gains in encoding efficiency and downstream language-model performance on domain-specific content without compromising general-language performance. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time
docs.text:
Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time Learning Positive Linear Combinations of ReLUs in Fully Polynomial Time arXiv:2610.32940v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: We study the fundamental problem of PAC learning positive linear combinations of $k$ arbitrary ReLU activations on $\mathbb{R}^d$ with respect to the Gaussian distribution, in $L_2$ loss. We give the first fully-polynomial time algorithm for this learning task. Specifically, our algorithm draws $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ samples, runs in $\mathrm{poly}(d, k, 1/\epsilon)$ time, and outputs a hypothesis that is $\epsilon$-close to the target concept with high probability. All prior algorithms for this problem require super-polynomial time in $k$ or $1/\epsilon$, or leverage strong well-conditioned assumptions on the weight matrix.
  On a technical level, our approach develops a novel boosting procedure of a ``weak'' learner that recovers the hidden weight vectors to constant error, in a list-decodable manner. To develop this ``weak'' learning procedure, we leverage implicit tensor computation techniques to construct a low-degree filtering procedure based on Hermite tensors of the target function. This procedure amplifies separation among (clusters of) weight vectors to learn each of them to constant error. We then argue that the same procedure can be used for improving the estimation of hidden weight vectors, using gradient descent-like updates on the Euclidean sphere. A crucial ingredient of our algorithm is a pruning approach that ensures only relevant vectors that approximate the hidden weight vectors at target accuracy are maintained by the algorithm. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs
docs.text:
If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs arXiv:2610.32941v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation
docs.text:
Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation Knowledge Distillation across Item and Code Spaces for Parallel Generative Recommendation arXiv:2610.32943v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Generative recommendation with semantic IDs represents each item as a sequence of discrete codes derived from its semantic representation and predicts these codes to generate recommendations. Existing semantic-ID recommenders are typically trained with hard labels for the observed next item. Although such supervision identifies the target, it provides no explicit distributional information about alternative items conditioned on the same user history. Sequential recommenders can supply this item-level predictive knowledge, but transferring it to semantic-ID generation is challenging because the teacher and student operate in item and code spaces, respectively. We propose two complementary knowledge-distillation objectives for parallel semantic-ID recommenders, which predict all code positions simultaneously without autoregressive prefix conditioning. Item Distribution Matching (IDM) reconstructs a catalogue-level item distribution from the student's parallel code predictions and aligns it with the teacher's item distribution. Code Marginal Matching (CMM) projects the teacher's item probabilities onto each code position using fixed item-to-code assignments, then matches the resulting code marginals to the corresponding student heads. Both objectives transfer the teacher's soft distributional knowledge while preserving the student's parallel prediction structure. Experiments on benchmark datasets show that both methods consistently outperform existing state-of-the-art approaches. On average, IDM improves Recall@10 by 15.39%, while CMM improves NDCG@10 by 8.28%. These results demonstrate that distillation in either reconstructed item space or code-marginal space can substantially strengthen hard-label supervision for parallel generative recommendation. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox
docs.text:
Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox Measure Before You Train: Typed Decision Models vs. a Classical Baseline vs. a Generative LLM for Routing a Personal Multilingual Inbox arXiv:2610.32955v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Personal email agents decide, for every message, what it is, whether it is urgent, whether to draft a reply, create a task, or ignore it. Their error rate is rarely measured: the stored labels were written by the system itself. We present Foyer, a self-hosted personal inbox agent in daily use, and a measurement protocol (stratified sampling, frozen snapshots, thread-grouped splits, pre-registered hypotheses, human labels in the agent's review loop) that yields ground truth before any training. On 739 real Italian/English emails labelled by the owner (231 unbiased, 500 adversarially sampled), we compare nine systems under thread-grouped cross-validation: the production keyword rules, a TF-IDF + logistic-regression baseline, local typed decision models (Tev1, Nimble), a hosted decision model (Nimble v4-max), and hosted generative LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma 4 26B/31B). Four results. The production rules score 28% on message type against a 58% majority class: the field shown most prominently carried no information. With ~200 labels, logistic regression has the highest accuracy on every field (type 0.79, urgency 0.74, needs-reply 0.83, is-noise 0.90), though it never predicts the two rarest classes and is statistically tied with Gemma 4 on type; few-shot prompting does not close the gap. The sender's relationship (client, supplier, service) is recovered from other emails of the same contact with 98.6% accuracy where the contact has been seen, and is not inferable from a single message by any model: it belongs in the contact graph, not the prompt. Finally, accuracy is not the product metric: composed into actions, the most accurate system most often ignores emails needing action (18% vs 4% for the best LLM); a cost-chosen threshold on its noise probability halves that rate and makes it the cheapest system. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection
docs.text:
Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection Flownomaly: Single-Step Conditional-Mean Recovery for Few-Shot Anomaly Detection arXiv:2610.32964v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Few-shot industrial anomaly detection requires modeling category-specific normality from only a handful of defect-free images. Common approaches tie inference to stored exemplars, impose rigid linear structure, or risk reproducing anomalous content. Flownomaly instead casts the problem as normal-counterpart recovery in frozen DINOv2 feature space. Given normal supports, a velocity field is learned through conditional flow matching over frozen patch tokens to transport Gaussian noise toward normal features. Along straight paths, a single recovery step using one evaluation of the optimal field yields the posterior mean of the clean normal token without trajectory integration. The operating time governs how strongly recovery modifies a query token. With no anomalous validation samples available for tuning, a normal-only Jacobian gain-to-noise criterion selects this time from the supports alone. Squared residuals between query tokens and their recovered counterparts yield anomaly signals for both dense localization and image-level detection. Across 1-, 2-, and 4-shot benchmarks on MVTec-AD and VisA, together with sample-shot evaluations on Real-IAD, Flownomaly achieves state-of-the-art performance against recent category-specific methods. In the 1-shot setting, image- and pixel-level AUROC reach 97.8% and 98.0% on MVTec-AD and 95.3% and 98.7% on VisA, with a 2.1-point image-level AUROC improvement over the strongest baseline on VisA. Code is available at https://github.com/b-rbmp/Flownomaly. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection
docs.text:
DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection DexPort: A Hand-Held Skill Interface for Dexterous Hand Data Collection arXiv:2610.32969v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models
docs.text:
Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models Maximum Likelihood on the Joint (Data, Condition) Distribution for Solving Ill-Posed Problems with Conditional Flow Models arXiv:2208.11782v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In the absence of conditioning information, normalizing flow models are trained using maximum likelihood. Previous extensions to conditional settings have abandoned the simple maximum-likelihood approach, as obtaining the full joint distribution of data and conditions for training purposes (or equivalently, the true conditional distribution for each point in the training dataset) is impossible. However, under special conditions that nevertheless apply to a wide class of useful problems, it is possible to obtain a simple, computationally cheap proxy with the same global minimum as the conditional likelihood. Conditional flow models trained using this proxy do not require explicit knowledge of the conditional distribution, auxiliary networks or other specific architecture, or additional loss terms beyond maximum likelihood. They provide a natural and powerful way to solve a class of ill-posed inverse problems. I demonstrate these properties on easily visualized toy problems, then use the method to successfully generate class-conditional images and to reconstruct semantically degraded images via super-resolution. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: FC-PINO: High Precision Physics-Informed Neural Operators via Fourier Continuation
docs.text:
FC-PINO: High Precision Physics-Informed Neural Operators via Fourier Continuation FC-PINO: High Precision Physics-Informed Neural Operators via Fourier Continuation arXiv:2211.15960v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: The physics-informed neural operator (PINO) is a machine learning paradigm that has demonstrated promising results for learning solutions to partial differential equations (PDEs). It leverages the Fourier Neural Operator to learn solution operators in function spaces and leverages physics losses during training to penalize deviations from known physics laws. Spectral differentiation provides an efficient way to compute derivatives for the physics losses, but it inherently assumes periodicity. When applied to non-periodic functions, this assumption can lead to significant errors, including Gibbs phenomena near domain boundaries which degrade the accuracy of both function representations and derivative computations. To overcome this limitation, we introduce the FC-PINO (Fourier-Continuation-based Physics-Informed Neural Operator) architecture which extends the accuracy and efficiency of PINO and spectral differentiation to non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs. In FC-PINO, we propose integrating Fourier continuation into the PINO framework, and test two different continuation approaches: FC-Legendre and FC-Gram. By transforming non-periodic signals into periodic functions on extended domains in a well-conditioned manner, Fourier continuation enables fast and accurate derivative computations. This approach avoids the discretization sensitivity of finite differences and the memory overhead of automatic differentiation. We demonstrate that standard PINO fails (without padding) or struggles (even with padding) to solve non-periodic and non-smooth PDEs with high precision, across challenging benchmarks. In contrast, the proposed FC-PINO provides accurate, robust, and scalable solutions, substantially outperforming PINO alternatives, and demonstrating that Fourier continuation is critical for extending PINO to a wider range of PDE problems when high-precision solutions are needed. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Learning from Hypervectors: A Survey on Hyperdimensional Encoding
docs.text:
Learning from Hypervectors: A Survey on Hyperdimensional Encoding Learning from Hypervectors: A Survey on Hyperdimensional Encoding arXiv:2308.00685v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Hyperdimensional computing (HDC) is an emerging computing paradigm that imitates the brain's structure to offer a powerful and efficient processing and learning model. In HDC, the data are encoded with long vectors, called hypervectors, which typically range from 1,000 to 10,000 in length. The literature provides several encoding methods to generate orthogonal or correlated hypervectors, based on the application. Existing surveys focus on overall HDC system aspects like inputs, primary computations, and outputs. However, this study takes a more specific approach. It zeroes in on the HDC system input and the generation of hypervectors, directly influencing the hypervector encoding. This survey brings together various hypervector generation and encoding methods, exploring the limitations, challenges, and potential benefits they entail. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Catastrophic Overfitting, Entropy Gap and Participation Ratio: A Noiseless $l^p$ Norm Solution for Fast Adversarial Training
docs.text:
Catastrophic Overfitting, Entropy Gap and Participation Ratio: A Noiseless $l^p$ Norm Solution for Fast Adversarial Training Catastrophic Overfitting, Entropy Gap and Participation Ratio: A Noiseless $l^p$ Norm Solution for Fast Adversarial Training arXiv:2505.02360v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Adversarial training is a cornerstone of robust deep learning, but fast methods like the Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM) often suffer from Catastrophic Overfitting (CO), where models become robust to single-step attacks but fail against multi-step variants. While existing solutions rely on noise injection, regularization, or gradient clipping, we propose a novel solution that purely controls the $l^p$ training norm to mitigate CO. Our study is motivated by the empirical observation that CO is more prevalent under the $l^{\infty}$ norm than the $l^2$ norm. Leveraging this insight, we develop a framework for generalized $l^p$ attack as a fixed point problem and craft $l^p$-FGSM attacks to understand the transition mechanics from $l^2$ to $l^{\infty}$. This leads to our core insight: CO emerges when highly concentrated gradients, where information localizes in few dimensions, interact with aggressive norm constraints. By quantifying gradient concentration through Participation Ratio and entropy measures, we develop an adaptive $l^p$-FGSM that automatically tunes the training norm based on gradient information. Extensive experiments demonstrate that this approach achieves competitive robustness without requiring additional regularization or noise injection, providing a novel and theoretically-principled pathway to mitigate the CO problem. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback
docs.text:
From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback From Dueling Bandits to Episodic MDPs: Learning with Adversarial Preference Feedback arXiv:2507.11706v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In dueling bandits, the learner compares two arms in each round and observes only which one is preferred. This paper asks what changes when the compared pair also affects the next state, as in a recommendation interface where the pair shown to a user affects the user's next context. We formulate this problem as a state-wise preference-based MDP, an episodic tabular MDP in which the learner selects a pair of arms at each visited state, observes only a noisy comparison between them, and moves to a next state that may depend on the pair. The preferences may change adversarially across episodes, and the loss of a pair is defined through Borda scores. We show that the minimax regret of this problem under known transitions is $\tilde{\Theta}(\min\{HT,(H^3SK)^{1/3}T^{2/3}\})$, where $H$, $S$, $K$, and $T$ are the numbers of steps per episode, states, arms, and episodes, and that this rate is achieved by an algorithm based on online linear optimization over the set of occupancy measures. If the pair did not affect the next state, each state would be a separate dueling bandit, and the $T^{2/3}$ term of the minimax regret would be smaller by a factor of $H^{1/3}$, demonstrating the cost of having action-dependent state transitions. We also give a policy optimization algorithm with closed-form updates, whose regret is $\tilde{O}((H^4SK^3)^{1/3}T^{2/3})$ up to lower-order terms, and we extend both algorithms to unknown transitions. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Dynamic Relational Priming Improves Transformer in Multivariate Time Series
docs.text:
Dynamic Relational Priming Improves Transformer in Multivariate Time Series Dynamic Relational Priming Improves Transformer in Multivariate Time Series arXiv:2509.12196v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Standard attention mechanisms in transformers employ static token representations that remain unchanged across all pair-wise computations in each layer. This limits their representational alignment with the potentially diverse relational dynamics of each token-pair interaction. While they excel in domains with relatively homogeneous relationships, standard attention's static relational learning struggles to capture the diverse, heterogeneous inter-channel dependencies of multivariate time series (MTS) data--where different channel-pair interactions within a single system may be governed by entirely different physical laws or temporal dynamics. To better align the attention mechanism for such domain phenomena, we propose attention with dynamic relational priming (prime attention). Unlike standard attention where each token presents an identical representation across all of its pair-wise interactions, prime attention tailors each token dynamically (or per interaction) through learnable modulations to best capture the unique relational dynamics of each token pair, optimizing each pair-wise interaction for that specific relationship. This representational plasticity of prime attention enables effective extraction of relationship-specific information in MTS while maintaining the same asymptotic computational complexity as standard attention. Our results demonstrate that prime attention consistently outperforms standard attention across benchmarks, achieving up to 6.5\% improvement in forecasting accuracy. In addition, we find that prime attention achieves comparable or superior performance using up to 40\% less sequence length compared to standard attention, further demonstrating its superior relational modeling capabilities. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Clip-Low Increases Entropy and Clip-High Decreases Entropy in Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models
docs.text:
Clip-Low Increases Entropy and Clip-High Decreases Entropy in Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models Clip-Low Increases Entropy and Clip-High Decreases Entropy in Reinforcement Learning of Large Language Models arXiv:2509.26114v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has recently emerged as the leading approach for enhancing the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, RLVR is prone to entropy collapse, where the LLM quickly converges to a near-deterministic form, hindering exploration and progress during prolonged RL training. In this work, we reveal that the clipping mechanism in PPO and GRPO induces biases on entropy. Through theoretical and empirical analyses, we show that clip-low increases entropy, while clip-high decreases it. Further, under standard clipping parameters, the effect of clip-high dominates, resulting in an overall entropy reduction even when purely random rewards are provided to the RL algorithm. Our findings highlight an overlooked confounding factor in RLVR: independent of the reward signal, the clipping mechanism influences entropy, which in turn affects the reasoning behavior. Furthermore, our analysis demonstrates that clipping can be deliberately used to control entropy. Specifically, with a more aggressive clip-low value, one can increase entropy, promote exploration, and ultimately prevent entropy collapse in RLVR training. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL
docs.text:
Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL arXiv:2511.21638v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Practical LLM agents often operate over multi-turn conversations where success is determined only after the full interaction ends. Most multi-turn RL methods train via on-policy rollouts, but unlike in single-turn RL, the policy cannot produce a trajectory alone, since an external environment must respond after each agent turn. For conversational agents, this environment is a user, but real users are generally unavailable inside the training loop and simulated users are difficult to build faithfully. Separately, real-world deployment is rarely fully online or fully offline. The common production pattern is called batch online, where the current policy is deployed to collect a batch of interaction data, then retrained on that batch and redeployed. We show that this batch-online setting creates an opportunity for applying the classical approximate policy iteration algorithm. Our central observation is that running standard token-level, single-turn GRPO with a learned turn-level $Q$-function as the reward model is a policy improvement step for the multi-turn problem. Building on this, we present Iterative Policy Optimization (IterPO), which alternates between fitting $Q^\pi$ from logged Monte Carlo returns via standard reward modeling (policy evaluation) and running single-turn GRPO against $Q^\pi$ (policy improvement). During policy improvement, the learned $Q^\pi$ scores candidate responses by their expected downstream return, avoiding the need for simulator rollouts of the remaining conversation. Overall, this allows us to do principled multi-turn RL using only single-turn RL methods without an interactive environment or user simulator inside the training loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IterPO on six multi-turn negotiation environments. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Softly Symbolifying Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
docs.text:
Softly Symbolifying Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks Softly Symbolifying Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks arXiv:2512.07875v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (KANs) offer a promising path toward interpretable machine learning: their learnable activations can be studied individually while collectively fitting complex data accurately. In practice, however, trained activations often lack *symbolic fidelity*, learning pathological decompositions with no meaningful correspondence to interpretable forms. We propose Softly Symbolified Kolmogorov--Arnold Networks (S2KAN), which integrate symbolic primitives directly into training. Each activation draws from a dictionary of symbolic and dense terms, with learnable gates that sparsify the representation. Crucially, this sparsification is differentiable, enabling end-to-end optimization, and uses an optimization objective inspired by minimum description length. S2KAN can discover interpretable activation functions while retaining dense splines for flexible approximation. We introduce a quantitative measure of symbolic fidelity, assessing how closely learned activations can be approximated by short expressions from a specified symbolic language. Across real-world prediction tasks, dynamical-system forecasting, and synthetic symbolic benchmarks, S2KAN generally achieves higher symbolic fidelity and often far smaller models, while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy on real-world data and low prediction errors on most symbolic benchmark configurations. We also examine the models' learned responses on scientific data, including the contributions of their symbolic components. Together, these results show that incorporating symbolic structure during training can yield compact, accurate KAN models whose learned responses can be examined through their symbolic components. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Multi-Task Learning for Metal Alloy Property Prediction: An Empirical Study of Negative Transfer and Mitigation Strategies
docs.text:
Multi-Task Learning for Metal Alloy Property Prediction: An Empirical Study of Negative Transfer and Mitigation Strategies Multi-Task Learning for Metal Alloy Property Prediction: An Empirical Study of Negative Transfer and Mitigation Strategies arXiv:2512.22740v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Multi-task learning (MTL) in materials science relies on the assumption that physically related properties share learnable representations. We challenge this assumption using a 54,028-sample metal alloy dataset exhibiting extreme task-level imbalance. Our results reveal a striking dichotomy: MTL significantly degrades regression performance for resistivity and hardness but improves classification recall for amorphous-forming ability. We trace this divergence to mismatched functional forms--such as resistivity's polynomial dependence versus hardness's complex interactions--which cause severe gradient misalignment during optimization. Evaluating Deep Imbalanced Regression techniques, we find that projecting conflicting gradients (PCGrad) recovers single-task performance, while combining label distribution smoothing with gradient normalization achieves the best overall balance. Consequently, we propose a strategic framework: utilize independent models for high-precision characterization, but employ MTL for high-throughput screening where recall is paramount. These findings support a "materials property clustering" hypothesis, suggesting that distinct physical mechanisms require specialized optimization strategies to overcome negative transfer. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling
docs.text:
On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling On the Runway Cascade of Transformers for Language Modeling arXiv:2601.14522v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: In decoder-only (causal) transformers, the computation graph created by causal masking routes information through both direct-path attention and indirect paths formed by intermediate tokens. We denote these indirect paths between token pairs as their runways. We argue that certain failure modes of causal transformers as observed by a growing body of recent works are likely exacerbated by a misalignment between these two information propagation modes. We formalize runway cascade as a phenomenon whereby this misalignment results in redundancies and irrelevant information cascading to token representations despite adequately learned attention patterns. As a solution, we propose runway-aware rewiring as a more explicit way of incorporating runway context directly into each token's direct-path attention. This mechanism re-wires the attention pattern for each token based on a summary of its runway landscape, enabling awareness of accumulating representational influences and allowing for more balanced information propagation. Our proposed methodology introduces no additional parameters and can seamlessly be integrated into standard attention mechanism. Empirically, our rewired transformer results in steady improvements in general language modeling as well as noticeably stronger information retrieval and extrapolation abilities compared to standard transformers. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Feature-Space Smoothing: Certified Robustness of Deep Representations
docs.text:
Feature-Space Smoothing: Certified Robustness of Deep Representations Feature-Space Smoothing: Certified Robustness of Deep Representations arXiv:2601.16200v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern deep learning models exhibit strong capabilities across diverse applications, yet remain vulnerable to malicious inputs that induce erroneous predictions via feature-space distortion. To address that, we propose Feature-Space Smoothing (FS), a representation-level certification framework built upon Gaussian randomized smoothing. We show that FS converts a given feature encoder into a smoothed variant that is guaranteed to maintain a certified lower bound on the cosine similarity between clean and adversarial features under l_2-bounded perturbations. We then establish that this Feature Cosine Similarity Bound (FCSB) can be extended to the prediction-wise certification under the cosine similarity measure, and the value of FCSB is determined by the encoder intrinsic Gaussian robustness score. Building on those insights, we introduce the Gaussian Smoothness Booster (GSB), a plug-and-play module to improve the encoder Gaussian robustness score. Specifically, the GSB module is plugged to enhance the feature-space consistency and maintain the feature utility for downstream tasks under Gaussian perturbations. This design enables seamless integration of FS on the protected model, e.g., Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), without additional model retraining or alignment, improving its robustness while preserving the performance for downstream task-oriented decoding. Extensive experiments demonstrate that integrating FS consistently provides non-trivial certified robustness and significantly improves task-oriented performance under strong white-box adversarial attacks across diverse models and applications. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Clifford Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
docs.text:
Clifford Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks Clifford Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks arXiv:2602.05977v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Clifford Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (ClKAN), a flexible and efficient architecture for function approximation in arbitrary Clifford Algebra spaces. We propose the use of Randomized Quasi-Monte Carlo grid generation as a solution to the exponential scaling associated with higher-dimensional algebras. Our ClKAN also introduces new batch normalization strategies to deal with variable domain input. ClKAN finds application in scientific discovery and engineering, and is validated in synthetic and physics-inspired tasks. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: StealthRL: Reinforcement Learning Paraphrase Attacks for Multi-Detector Evasion of AI-Text Detectors
docs.text:
StealthRL: Reinforcement Learning Paraphrase Attacks for Multi-Detector Evasion of AI-Text Detectors StealthRL: Reinforcement Learning Paraphrase Attacks for Multi-Detector Evasion of AI-Text Detectors arXiv:2602.08934v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: AI-text detectors are increasingly used in high-stakes settings, but their robustness to meaning-preserving adversarial rewriting remains unclear. We introduce StealthRL, a reinforcement learning framework for stress-testing detectors with adaptive paraphrase attacks. StealthRL trains a paraphrase policy against a detector ensemble while enforcing semantic fidelity, then evaluates transfer to held-out detector families on the full filtered MAGE test pool. Across RoBERTa, Fast-DetectGPT, Binoculars, and MAGE, the resulting attack sharply degrades detection performance, driving mean TPR@1%FPR down to 0.024 while retaining nontrivial semantic overlap and readable prose. The attack also transfers to detectors not used during training, indicating a broader robustness failure rather than overfitting to a single target model. We complement the main results with detector-score analysis, repeated-generation stability checks, and automatic and judge-based quality evaluation. Our findings suggest that current AI-text detectors remain brittle under adaptive paraphrasing pressure and motivate robustness evaluation at deployment-relevant operating points. Our code and the trained model checkpoint are publicly available. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Mitigating the Likelihood Paradox in Flow-based OOD Detection: An Entropic Perspective
docs.text:
Mitigating the Likelihood Paradox in Flow-based OOD Detection: An Entropic Perspective Mitigating the Likelihood Paradox in Flow-based OOD Detection: An Entropic Perspective arXiv:2602.09581v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep generative models that can tractably compute input likelihoods, including normalizing flows, often assign unexpectedly high likelihoods to out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. We mitigate this paradox from an entropic perspective with Semantic Proportional Entropy Manipulation (SPEM), a training-free procedure that applies stronger perturbations to inputs less similar to an in-distribution (ID) memory bank. We derive theoretical lower bounds showing that this entropy gap increases the expected log-likelihood difference in favor of the ID, and experiments on standard benchmarks show that this manipulation realigns the likelihood ordering with human intuition. Strikingly, this realignment persists even when the flow is given only visually meaningless noise instead of the original input, and we analyze this phenomenon theoretically to characterize the conditions under which it occurs. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Why Does Counterintuitive Likelihood Behavior Rarely Emerge in Tabular Anomaly Detection?
docs.text:
Why Does Counterintuitive Likelihood Behavior Rarely Emerge in Tabular Anomaly Detection? Why Does Counterintuitive Likelihood Behavior Rarely Emerge in Tabular Anomaly Detection? arXiv:2602.09593v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Deep generative models with tractable likelihoods, exemplified by normalizing flows, offer an effective basis for anomaly detection through likelihood-based scoring. We demonstrate that, unlike in the image domain where deep generative models frequently assign higher likelihoods to anomalous data, such counterintuitive behavior occurs rarely in tabular settings. We first introduce a domain-agnostic formulation that enables consistent detection and evaluation of the counterintuitive phenomenon, addressing the lack of a precise definition in prior work. Through extensive experiments on 47 tabular datasets benchmarked against 13 baseline models and on 10 CV/NLP embedding datasets from ADBench, we show that the phenomenon is consistently rare in general tabular data and that normalizing flow likelihood achieves competitive anomaly detection performance. We further provide theoretical and empirical analyses attributing this disparity to differences in dimensionality and feature correlation between tabular and image data. Therefore, our results indicate that likelihood-based detection with normalizing flows is a practical approach for tabular anomaly detection. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning
docs.text:
Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning arXiv:2603.02604v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We introduce Heterogeneous Agent Collaborative Reinforcement Learning (HACRL), a new Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Reward (RLVR) problem that addresses the inefficiencies of isolated multi-agent on-policy optimization. HACRL enables collaborative optimization with independent execution: heterogeneous agents share verified rollouts during training to mutually improve, while operating independently at inference time. Unlike LLM-based multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL), HACRL does not require coordinated deployment, and unlike on-/off-policy distillation, it enables bidirectional mutual learning among heterogeneous agents rather than one-directional homogeneous teacher-to-student transfer. Building on this problem, we propose HACPO, a collaborative RL algorithm that enables principled rollout sharing to maximize sample utilization and cross-agent knowledge transfer. To mitigate capability discrepancies and policy distribution shifts, HACPO introduces four tailored mechanisms with theoretical guarantees on unbiased advantage estimation. Extensive experiments across diverse heterogeneous model combinations and reasoning benchmarks show that HACPO consistently improves all participating agents, outperforming GSPO with double rollouts by an average of 3.6% while using only half the rollout cost. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios
docs.text:
MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios MoE-SpAc: Efficient MoE Inference Based on Speculative Activation Utility in Heterogeneous Edge Scenarios arXiv:2603.09983v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models enable scalable performance but face severe memory constraints on edge devices. Existing offloading strategies struggle with I/O bottlenecks due to the dynamic, low-information nature of autoregressive expert activation. In this paper, we propose to repurpose Speculative Decoding (SD) not merely as a compute accelerator, but as an informative lookahead sensor for memory management, supported by our theoretical and empirical analyses. Hence, we introduce MoE-SpAc, an MoE inference framework that integrates a Speculative Utility Estimator to track expert demand, a Heterogeneous Workload Balancer to dynamically partition computation via online integer optimization, and an Asynchronous Execution Engine to unify the prefetching and eviction in the same utility space. Extensive experiments on seven benchmarks demonstrate that MoE-SpAc achieves a 42% improvement in TPS over the SOTA SD-based baseline, and an average 4.04x speedup over all standard baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/lshAlgorithm/MoE-SpAc . アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: VLMShield: Efficient and Robust Defense of Vision-Language Models against Malicious Prompts
docs.text:
VLMShield: Efficient and Robust Defense of Vision-Language Models against Malicious Prompts VLMShield: Efficient and Robust Defense of Vision-Language Models against Malicious Prompts arXiv:2604.06502v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) face significant safety vulnerabilities from malicious prompt attacks due to weakened alignment during visual integration. Existing defenses suffer from efficiency and robustness. To address these challenges, we first propose the Multimodal Aggregated Feature Extraction (MAFE) framework that enables CLIP to handle long text and fuse multimodal information into unified representations. Through empirical analysis of MAFE-extracted features, we discover distinct distributional patterns between benign and malicious prompts. Building upon this finding, we develop VLMShield, a lightweight safety detector that efficiently identifies multimodal malicious attacks as a plug-and-play solution. Extensive experiments demonstrate superior performance across multiple dimensions, including robustness, efficiency, and utility. Through our work, we hope to pave the way for more secure multimodal AI deployment. Code is available at [this https URL](https://github.com/pgqihere/VLMShield). アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: MoLS: SNR-Guided Module-Wise Learning-Rate Calibration for Large Language Models
docs.text:
MoLS: SNR-Guided Module-Wise Learning-Rate Calibration for Large Language Models MoLS: SNR-Guided Module-Wise Learning-Rate Calibration for Large Language Models arXiv:2605.05794v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) contain functionally distinct modules with heterogeneous gradient statistics. Although Adam(W) adapts updates at the parameter level, selecting relative learning rates across modules often relies on costly manual tuning. We study this problem through gradient signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Our analysis identifies structural sources of module-wise SNR differences and relates SNR to the attenuation of Adam's normalized mean-gradient component. Based on these findings, we propose \textbf{Module-wise Learning Rate Scaling via SNR (\name)}, a lightweight method that replaces manual multiplier search with one-shot calibration. MoLS estimates module-level SNRs after an initial adaptation period and uses inverse-square-root scaling to determine relative learning-rate multipliers. The multipliers are introduced smoothly during warmup and then held fixed while the global learning-rate schedule continues. Our theoretical results quantify the effect of calibration and its sensitivity to estimation error and relative SNR drift. Extensive experiments across LLM pre-training and fine-tuning show that MoLS reduces perplexity and improves downstream accuracy with minimal computational overhead. It achieves performance comparable to carefully tuned module-specific learning rates and integrates with memory-efficient optimizers and parameter-efficient fine-tuning. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Q-MMR: Off-Policy Evaluation via Recursive Reweighting and Moment Matching
docs.text:
Q-MMR: Off-Policy Evaluation via Recursive Reweighting and Moment Matching Q-MMR: Off-Policy Evaluation via Recursive Reweighting and Moment Matching arXiv:2605.06474v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We present a novel theoretical framework, Q-MMR, for off-policy evaluation in finite-horizon MDPs. Q-MMR learns a set of scalar weights, one for each data point, such that the reweighted rewards approximate the expected return under the target policy. The weights are learned inductively in a top-down manner via a moment matching objective against a value-function discriminator class. Notably, and perhaps surprisingly, a data-dependent finite-sample guarantee for general function approximation can be established under only the realizability of $Q^\pi$, with a dimension-free bound -- that is, the error does not depend on the statistical complexity of the function class. We also establish connections to several existing methods, such as importance sampling and linear FQE. Further theoretical analyses shed new light on the nature of coverage, a concept of fundamental importance to offline RL. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: POETS: Uncertainty-Aware LLM Optimization via Compute-Efficient Policy Ensembles
docs.text:
POETS: Uncertainty-Aware LLM Optimization via Compute-Efficient Policy Ensembles POETS: Uncertainty-Aware LLM Optimization via Compute-Efficient Policy Ensembles arXiv:2605.07775v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Balancing exploration with exploitation is a core challenge in black-box optimization and reinforcement learning. We introduce POETS ($\textbf{Po}$licy $\textbf{E}$nsembles for $\textbf{T}$hompson $\textbf{S}$ampling), a novel framework that bridges uncertainty quantification and policy optimization. Our approach is grounded in the insight that policies trained with Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization implicitly encode an underlying reward function. Building on this, POETS bypasses the complex, nested process of training an uncertainty-aware reward model and separately fitting a policy to this model. Instead, we directly train a policy ensemble to capture epistemic uncertainty by matching implicitly encoded reward functions to online, bootstrapped data. To overcome the prohibitive compute and memory constraints of ensembling Large Language Models (LLMs), POETS utilizes an efficient architecture: the ensemble shares a pre-trained backbone while maintaining diversity through independent Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) branches. Theoretically, we show that POETS implicitly approximates KL-regularized Thompson sampling, a principled optimization strategy with optimal cumulative regret bounds of $O(\sqrt{T \gamma_T})$. Empirically, we demonstrate that POETS achieves state-of-the-art sample efficiency across diverse scientific discovery domains, including protein search, therapeutic molecular design, and quantum circuit design. POETS also improves the optimization trajectory and out-of-distribution transfer of reinforcement learning across mathematical reasoning and code generation tasks, proving particularly robust in off-policy settings with experience replay or in small dataset regimes. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Generalized Wasserstein Flow Matching: Nested Couplings for Point Cloud Generation
docs.text:
Generalized Wasserstein Flow Matching: Nested Couplings for Point Cloud Generation Generalized Wasserstein Flow Matching: Nested Couplings for Point Cloud Generation arXiv:2605.08424v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We formulate flow matching on probability measures over probability measures. Directly from the Wasserstein-on-Wasserstein (WoW) continuity equation, we show that admissible nested outer and inner couplings induce a valid metameasure flow and non-local velocity field. Validity requires neither optimal plans nor a smooth manifold. Practically, this opens up the design space of multisample flow matching: exact Wasserstein plans are distinguished by energy and straightness, while sliced and lazy linear plans yield scalable alternatives. Point-cloud experiments, including controlled Bures-Wasserstein and Euclidean minibatch baselines, demonstrate the resulting geometry-cost trade-off. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: U-STS-LLM: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Steered Large Language Model for Traffic Prediction and Imputation
docs.text:
U-STS-LLM: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Steered Large Language Model for Traffic Prediction and Imputation U-STS-LLM: A Unified Spatio-Temporal Steered Large Language Model for Traffic Prediction and Imputation arXiv:2605.11735v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Accurate spatio-temporal cellular traffic analysis is fundamental to the reliable operation of modern mobile networks, as it underpins load forecasting for congestion avoidance and missing-data imputation for continuity despite transmission errors. While deeply connected, forecasting and imputation have historically evolved as separate sub-fields. Existing models are typically task-specific, decouple temporal and spatial modeling, and rely on cascaded designs that accumulate errors and latency. Meanwhile, adapting pre-trained LLMs for this domain often leaves spatial structure under-guided and tends to overfit on limited data. To bridge these gaps, we propose U-STS-LLM, a unified framework built on a partially frozen spatio-temporally attentive (PFSTA) LLM backbone. A Dynamic Spatio-Temporal Attention Bias Generator synthesizes a persistent functional graph with transient nodal states to steer attention, while a lightweight parallel branch yields a stable local estimate fused via a Gated Adaptive Fusion, confining the LLM to residual correction. Trained under a unified multi-task objective, the model attains state-of-the-art results with low trainable-parameter overhead. Extensive experiments on real-world cellular traffic datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of U-STS-LLM, achieving average RMSE improvements of 23.7% over the strongest baselines in forecasting and 13.1% in imputation, with further gains exceeding 33% in zero-shot transfer to unseen network regions. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: NodeSyn: Socially Aligned Synthetic Data for AI Evaluation
docs.text:
NodeSyn: Socially Aligned Synthetic Data for AI Evaluation NodeSyn: Socially Aligned Synthetic Data for AI Evaluation arXiv:2605.14381v4 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Recent advancements in generative AI facilitate large-scale synthetic data generation for model evaluation. However, without targeted approaches, these datasets often lack the sociotechnical nuance required for sensitive domains. We introduce NodeSyn, a methodology that pairs a fine-tuned taxonomy generator (TaG) with credible published sources and extracted sensitive attributes to generate queries reflecting authentic societal contexts and nuanced harms. Evaluated across ten open-weight and proprietary LLMs in Medical Advice and Self-Harm using human-validated autoraters, NodeSyn ranked first on 8 of 10 models in each domain. NodeSyn datasets induced average failure rates 3.1 times higher than generic synthetic baselines, 2.4 times higher than structured synthetic benchmarks, and 1.6 times higher than authentic human-authored queries. Ablation studies confirm that, controlling for structural confounds, our granular Level 3 taxonomic expansion significantly drives these failure rates over Level 2 across 9 of 10 models (+29.2% relative lift in Medical Advice and +24.0% in Self-Harm). Variance attribution analysis reveals that failures are driven not only by what topics are queried (taxonomic nodes and lexical specificity), but also by their sociotechnical grounding (affected demographics, occupations, geographies, and querying personas). We embed this method into a research prototype, and open-source (https://github.com/google-research/nodesynth) the code and datasets to enable scalable, high-stakes model evaluation. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Risk Prediction: A Dedicated Review and Empirical Comparison
docs.text:
Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Risk Prediction: A Dedicated Review and Empirical Comparison Tabular Foundation Models for Credit Risk Prediction: A Dedicated Review and Empirical Comparison arXiv:2605.18147v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Predictive models are central to credit risk management, where the accuracy of default-probability and loss estimates affects the profitability of lending and the stability of the financial system. Decades of benchmarking research have consolidated the state of the art, with gradient-boosting models often representing the strongest machine-learning benchmark, while linear and logistic models remain important regulatory and industry reference models. The recent advent of tabular data foundation models introduces a new paradigm for predictive modeling. Rather than fitting a model to a target dataset, they use in-context learning to integrate information from the target dataset with prior knowledge acquired through large-scale pretraining on diverse collections of (synthetic) tabular data. We conjecture that access to information beyond the target data is beneficial in small-data settings and may help address longstanding challenges, including low-default portfolios. Whether this promise holds in practice remains an open question. This paper benchmarks state-of-the-art tabular foundation models against a broad set of classical and advanced machine learning competitors on two core tasks: Probability of Default (PD) and Loss Given Default (LGD) modeling. We evaluate $33$ classification methods across $14$ PD datasets and $27$ regression methods across $7$ LGD datasets, spanning a range of performance indicators and experimental conditions. The most recent tabular foundation models, in particular TabPFN-3 and TabICLv2, achieve the strongest average results, with the largest gains in small-sample and strongly imbalanced settings. These results are notable because these models are used with their pretrained parameters fixed and without downstream hyperparameter optimization or task-specific parameter updates. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Shaping the Prior: How Synthetic Task Distributions Determine Tabular Foundation Model Quality
docs.text:
Shaping the Prior: How Synthetic Task Distributions Determine Tabular Foundation Model Quality Shaping the Prior: How Synthetic Task Distributions Determine Tabular Foundation Model Quality arXiv:2605.18971v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: What determines the quality of a tabular foundation model? Unlike language or vision, tabular foundation models acquire their inductive biases almost entirely from synthetic pretraining distributions, yet the design of these distributions remains poorly understood. Standard synthetic priors are too well-behaved: they omit the irregularities and failure modes that determine deployment robustness. We introduce O'Prior, a compositional realism prior built around four coupled components: a hierarchical SCM meta-generator spanning diverse functional families; a modular realism engine covering heterogeneous marginals, missingness, and target transforms; an explicit stress module injecting confounding and support-query mismatch; and a curriculum-governed, leakage-safe generation protocol. To isolate prior design as the scientific variable, we hold architecture, optimizer, and compute budget fixed and vary only the synthetic task distribution. O'Prior yields consistent and substantial improvements in downstream accuracy and robustness across real tabular benchmarks, with gains concentrated in regimes characterized by distributional irregularities. Ablations confirm that mechanism diversity, realism composition, and shift-aware stress each contribute independently, their effects are not interchangeable. These results establish synthetic prior construction as a first-order and largely overlooked determinant of tabular foundation model quality. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Regret-Based $(\epsilon,\delta)$-optimal Stopping Criteria for Bayesian Optimization
docs.text:
Regret-Based $(\epsilon,\delta)$-optimal Stopping Criteria for Bayesian Optimization Regret-Based $(\epsilon,\delta)$-optimal Stopping Criteria for Bayesian Optimization arXiv:2605.22561v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Bayesian optimization (BO) is a widely used iterative black-box optimization method that utilizes Gaussian process (GP) surrogate models. In practice, BO is typically terminated after a fixed evaluation budget is exhausted, which can incur unnecessary cost and provides no optimality guarantee on solution quality. Recent research in developing a practical stopping criterion has made empirical progress, yet a theoretically sound stopping criterion remains a work in progress. In this work, we present provably tighter instantaneous regret bounds for GP upper confidence bound (GP-UCB) at any given iteration. Then, we propose stopping criteria for GP-UCB based on this tighter bound that ensures an $\epsilon$-optimal solution with high probability $1-\delta$ upon termination. Numerical experiments are performed to validate and demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of our stopping criteria. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Approaching I/O-optimality for Approximate Attention
docs.text:
Approaching I/O-optimality for Approximate Attention Approaching I/O-optimality for Approximate Attention arXiv:2605.23751v2 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: We revisit the I/O complexity of attention in large language models. Given query-key-value matrices $Q,K,V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, and a machine with fast memory size $M$, the goal is to compute the "attention matrix" $A=\text{softmax}(Q K ^{\top}/\sqrt{d}) V$ with the minimal number of data transfers between fast and slow memory. Existing methods in the literature, most notably FlashAttention and its variants, incur an I/O cost that depends quadratically on the context length $n$, while a trivial lower bound only requires $\Omega(nd)$ I/O's to read the inputs and write the output. In this work we show that the dependence on $n$ can be reduced to almost-linear, by developing I/O-efficient algorithms inspired by the recent approximate attention method of Alman and Song [NeurIPS'23]. We also provide (algorithm-specific) lower bounds in different parameter regimes, which nearly match the corresponding upper bounds, indicating that the proposed algorithms are indeed close to I/O-optimal. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones?
docs.text:
SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones? SoundnessBench: Can Your AI Scientist Really Tell Good Research Ideas from Bad Ones? arXiv:2605.30329v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Autonomous AI research agents aim to speed up scientific discovery by automating the research pipeline from hypothesis generation to peer review. However, existing benchmarks rarely test a fundamental bottleneck whether LLMs can judge the methodological viability of a research idea $\textbf{before}$ investing time and computational resources. Without a reliable ``first-gate'' filter, autonomous agents risk scaling flawed methodology rather than accelerating meaningful science. We introduce $\textbf{SoundnessBench}$, a curated benchmark of 1,099 real research proposals, with source verified extraction, reviewer-derived proxy labels, and proposal-only expert judgments on a subset of 327 proposals. Across 12 frontier LLMs, our evaluation reveals a pervasive $\textbf{optimism bias}$: standard prompting yields a $74.0\%$ mean false-positive rate. Aggressive prompting reduces false approvals but substantially increases false rejections. Additional analyses show that optimism persists under controls for public corpus contamination, and surface features, as well as in literature-grounded agent evaluation. These results suggest a limitation in judging scientific soundness, indicating that current LLMs are not yet reliable as standalone gatekeepers for scientific rigor. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Efficient Exploration for Iterative Nash Preference Optimization
docs.text:
Efficient Exploration for Iterative Nash Preference Optimization Efficient Exploration for Iterative Nash Preference Optimization arXiv:2606.01382v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Preference alignment is central to improving large language models (LLMs), but reward-based formulations can be restrictive when human preferences are non-transitive. Nash learning from human feedback (NLHF) addresses this limitation by modeling alignment as a preference game and seeking a Nash equilibrium. However, the learning-theoretic foundations of scalable NLHF remain limited: existing regret guarantees rely on explicit preference-model estimation and minimax oracles, whereas simpler iterative methods lack such guarantees. We study online iterative NLHF and identify exploration as a key obstacle. First, we show that standard iterative NLHF can incur an exponential dependence on the inverse KL-regularization parameter, demonstrating that implicit exploration through policy updates can be insufficient. We then propose Exploratory Nash Preference Optimization (ENPO), which combines a SFT-type regularization with adversarial policy exploration. ENPO eliminates this exponential dependence without requiring minimax oracles or explicit preference-model estimation. We further introduce Bonus-Explorer ENPO (BENPO), which uses additional oracles to achieve an $O(\log T)$ regret bound. Finally, we develop Direct ENPO (DENPO), a practical variant of ENPO for fine-tuning LLMs. Experiments with Llama-3-8B-Instruct demonstrate consistent improvements over the evaluated RLHF and NLHF baselines across multiple benchmarks. アルゴリズム paper

docs.title: Transient Amplification in Cascaded Gradient Methods: Exact Minimax Laws and Tracking without Resonance
docs.text:
Transient Amplification in Cascaded Gradient Methods: Exact Minimax Laws and Tracking without Resonance Transient Amplification in Cascaded Gradient Methods: Exact Minimax Laws and Tracking without Resonance arXiv:2606.04031v3 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Leader-follower gradient iterations, including bilevel and two-time-scale methods, can exhibit large finite-time excursions despite asymptotic stability. For cascaded iterations with block matrix J = [[A,0],[C,D]], symmetric diagonal blocks of norm at most gamma < 1, and coupling norm at most c, we prove an exact, dimension-free minimax formula: at every horizon t, the worst-case amplification equals the spectral norm of [[gamma^t,0],[c t gamma^(t-1),gamma^t]], attained by an aligned two-dimensional quadratic.
